sections.title: Overview
sections.summary: This manual (FHWA-NHI-14-007) provides updated, comprehensive guidance for design and construction of soil nail walls for highway applications. It supersedes FHWA-IF-03-017 (Lazarte et al. 2003) and incorporates LRFD methodology consistent with AASHTO 2014. Soil nailing is a top-down in-situ reinforcement technique using steel bars grouted in drilled holes.
sections.body: This manual was developed to provide updated, comprehensive guidance for the design and construction of soil nail walls for highway applications. The manual supersedes the previous Soil Nail Walls manual (FHWA-IF-03-017, Lazarte et al. 2003) and incorporates current LRFD design methodology consistent with the AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications (AASHTO 2014). Soil nailing is an in-situ soil reinforcement technique in which steel reinforcing elements (soil nails) are installed into the ground, typically as an excavation proceeds from the top down.
key_points: Supersedes FHWA-IF-03-017 (Lazarte et al. 2003)
Incorporates LRFD methodology consistent with AASHTO 2014
Soil nailing is an in-situ reinforcement technique using steel reinforcing elements
Top-down construction sequence as excavation proceeds
Primary audience: geotechnical, structural, and highway engineers
sections.applicability: General introduction to the GEC-7 soil nail walls manual.

sections.title: Purpose of the Manual
sections.summary: Provides state-of-practice LRFD design and construction guidance for both permanent and temporary soil nail wall applications in highway infrastructure. Covers subsurface investigation, material selection, corrosion protection, construction inspection, and performance monitoring.
sections.body: The purpose of this manual is to provide comprehensive, state-of-practice guidance for the design and construction of soil nail walls used in highway infrastructure. The manual is intended for use by engineers responsible for design and construction of highway projects. It presents procedures consistent with LRFD methodology, and addresses both permanent and temporary soil nail wall applications. The manual also provides guidance on subsurface investigation, material selection, corrosion protection, construction inspection, and performance monitoring.
key_points: Comprehensive state-of-practice guidance for soil nail wall design and construction
Consistent with LRFD methodology per AASHTO 2014
Addresses both permanent and temporary applications
Covers subsurface investigation, materials, corrosion protection
Provides construction inspection and performance monitoring guidance
sections.applicability: All soil nail wall projects for highway structures.

sections.title: Definition of Soil Nails
sections.summary: Soil nails are closely spaced passive (not post-tensioned) steel bar inclusions installed in drilled, grouted holes at 10–20 degrees below horizontal. Reinforcing action is mobilized by ground deformation. The reinforced soil mass acts as a gravity retaining structure; shotcrete facing with WWM or rebar provides nail connectivity and prevents local raveling.
sections.body: Soil nails are closely spaced, passive inclusions installed in existing ground to support an excavation or stabilize a slope. They are passive elements because they are not post-tensioned at installation and their reinforcing action is mobilized as the ground deforms. Soil nails are typically steel bars (solid or hollow), installed at a slight downward inclination (typically 10 to 20 degrees from horizontal) in drilled holes that are then grouted. The reinforced soil mass behind the facing acts as a gravity retaining structure. The facing, typically shotcrete reinforced with welded wire mesh (WWM) or rebar, provides connectivity between nails and prevents local soil raveling.
key_points: Soil nails are closely spaced passive inclusions in existing ground
Not post-tensioned; reinforcing action mobilized by ground deformation
Typically steel bars (solid or hollow) installed at 10-20 degrees below horizontal
Installed in drilled holes that are grouted
Reinforced soil mass acts as a gravity retaining structure
Facing (typically shotcrete with WWM or rebar) provides connectivity
sections.applicability: Fundamental definition and concept of soil nailing technique.

sections.title: Background
sections.summary: Soil nailing originated from the New Austrian Tunneling Method (NATM) in the 1960s–1970s. The first documented soil nail wall was built in 1972 near Versailles, France. The first U.S. demonstration project was in 1986 at Cumberland Gap, Tennessee. FHWA research (1996–2003) produced the predecessor manual FHWA-IF-03-017; the technique is now one of the most common top-down earth retention systems.
sections.body: Soil nailing originated from the New Austrian Tunneling Method (NATM) used in the 1960s-1970s. The first documented soil nail wall was constructed in 1972 near Versailles, France, for an 18-m deep railroad cut. The technique was introduced in North America in the late 1970s. In the U.S., the first soil nail wall demonstration project was constructed in 1986 on a highway project in Cumberland Gap, Tennessee. FHWA-sponsored research programs (1996-2003) led to the first comprehensive design manual (FHWA-IF-03-017). The technique has since become one of the most commonly used top-down earth retention systems in transportation projects.
key_points: Originated from the New Austrian Tunneling Method (NATM) in the 1960s-1970s
First documented soil nail wall: 1972 near Versailles, France (18-m railroad cut)
Introduced in North America in the late 1970s
First U.S. demonstration project: 1986, Cumberland Gap, Tennessee
FHWA research programs (1996-2003) led to first design manual FHWA-IF-03-017
Leading documents: FHWA-IF-03-017 (2003), Clouterre (1991, France), BS 8006 (UK)

sections.title: Design Philosophy
sections.summary: Soil nail wall design uses LRFD per AASHTO (2014) with resistance factors back-calibrated from ASD safety factors. Overall (global) stability is a service limit state; geotechnical and structural checks are strength limit states; seismic design uses the extreme event limit state. Load factors come from AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications.
sections.body: This manual presents soil nail wall design using the LRFD methodology as specified in AASHTO (2014). Resistance factors have been back-calibrated from ASD-based factors of safety to maintain consistency with past successful practice. Load factors are obtained from the AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications. Overall stability is treated as a service limit state using a resistance factor approach, while other geotechnical and structural limit states are treated as strength limit states. Seismic design follows the extreme event limit state provisions.
key_points: LRFD methodology per AASHTO (2014)
Resistance factors back-calibrated from ASD-based safety factors
Load factors from AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications
Overall stability treated as service limit state
Geotechnical and structural checks treated as strength limit states
Seismic design follows extreme event limit state provisions
sections.applicability: Design philosophy applicable to all soil nail wall LRFD design.

sections.title: Document Organization
sections.summary: Ten chapters and seven appendices: Chapters 1–5 cover background, feasibility, materials, investigation, and mechanics; Chapter 6 provides step-by-step design procedures; Chapter 7 covers corrosion protection; Chapters 8–9 address contracting, inspection, and monitoring; Chapter 10 covers hollow bar soil nails. Appendices A–G include design examples.
sections.body: The manual is organized into ten chapters and seven appendices. Chapter 1 provides an introduction. Chapter 2 covers applications and feasibility evaluations. Chapter 3 addresses construction materials and methods. Chapter 4 discusses information required for design, including subsurface investigation and design parameter selection. Chapter 5 presents resisting mechanisms and limit states. Chapter 6 provides step-by-step design procedures. Chapter 7 covers corrosion protection. Chapter 8 discusses contracting approaches and specifications. Chapter 9 covers construction inspection and performance monitoring. Chapter 10 addresses considerations for hollow bar soil nails. Appendices A through G provide supplementary information including design examples.
key_points: 10 chapters and 7 appendices (A through G)
Chapters 1-5: background, feasibility, materials, investigation, mechanics
Chapter 6: step-by-step design procedures (core design chapter)
Chapter 7: corrosion protection
Chapters 8-9: contracting, inspection, and monitoring
Chapter 10: hollow bar soil nails
Appendices include design examples
sections.applicability: Organization and scope of the two-volume manual.
